grief.title: The right to grieve
grief.read:
Everyone tells you to be strong. So you smile, you go to work, and when someone asks, you say “I’m fine.” Then one evening, in the kitchen, you see the cup they loved, and something inside you comes loose.

When Seneca lost a friend he loved dearly, he wrote that he wept so hard he couldn’t hold himself back, and he wasn’t ashamed of it. Let the tears fall, he said, but don’t let them become a flood that carries you away.

People think Stoicism means feeling nothing. It doesn’t. Pushing grief down and drowning in it are both ways of running from the same thing: sitting face to face with it. The Stoic doesn’t deny the pain; they make room for it, but they don’t hand it the keys to the house.

Tears aren’t weakness; they’re proof that the love is still there.

Today you’re allowed to cry. And if the grief feels too heavy, asking a professional for support is a Stoic choice too.
grief.body: Set aside ten minutes for yourself. Think only about what you miss; don’t try to stop it or fix it. When the time is up, drink a glass of water and go back to your day.
grief.ask: When you made room for missing them today, what did you feel? Did anything change?

grief.title: It was on loan
grief.read:
Their number is still in your phone. You can’t delete it; deleting it feels like losing them a second time. “They were mine,” you say. “They were taken from me.”

Epictetus used to give his students a strange piece of advice: never say about anything, “I have lost it,” but “I have given it back.” Has someone you love gone? They were given back.

This sounds like cold comfort, but it’s the opposite. Whoever says “I lost it” is demanding an account for something stolen from them. Whoever says “I gave it back” is counting a gift that was by their side for a while.

When you return a book you borrowed from the library, you don’t get angry; the pages you read are yours now.

However long it lasted, that time was yours.
grief.body: Write down what the person or thing you lost gave you: a habit, a phrase, a look, a lesson. Not what was taken, but what was given.
grief.ask: Which of the things you wrote is still with you today?

grief.title: The years that remain
grief.read:
As that date on the calendar draws closer, a heaviness settles over you. Your mind keeps going back to the same day: the last conversation, the last look, the thing you never got to say.

Seneca wrote a letter to Marcia, who was still grieving years after losing her son. He didn’t tell her to let go of her grief; he only asked her to turn her gaze: don’t count the day you lost him, count the years you had with him.

This isn’t making the loss smaller. The last day is only one of the thousands of days you spent together. But pain treats it as if it were the whole story.

Someone who always opens a photo album from the last page never sees the rest.

Remembering the whole story, not just the ending, gives them back to you.
grief.body: Share a memory of them that you love with someone, or write it down. In detail: where were you, what did you talk about, what did you laugh at?
grief.ask: Where did the memory you recalled today take you: to pain, or to warmth?

grief.title: The wave
grief.read:
You’d been fine for a few days. Then a song came on in the supermarket, and you froze where you stood. “I thought it had passed,” you thought.

Grief isn’t a straight road; it comes in waves. When Seneca was in exile, he waited a while before writing a letter of consolation to his mother; he knew that touching a fresh wound would only make it bleed. Pain has its own rhythm too.

A wave that comes back doesn’t mean you’re standing still. Over time the waves grow further apart, but sometimes one rises without warning. That isn’t failure; it’s a sign that the love is still alive.

Someone swimming in the sea doesn’t fight the wave; they hold their breath, go under it, and come back up to the surface.

The wave will come and it will pass. And you’ll still be on the shore.
grief.body: Notice the moment your grief rises. What set it off: a smell, a place, a time of day? Without running from it, just name it: “This is a wave.”
grief.ask: Did a wave come today? What did you do when you noticed it?

grief.title: Someone else’s grief
grief.read:
It’s as if your loss has shut you in a room. You think no one understands; the more you try to explain, the lonelier you feel.

Yet there are others living through the same loss: a sibling, a friend, someone who sat at the same table. They’re in their own rooms too, maybe waiting for a knock on your door.

The Stoics saw each person as part of a whole; the pain of one limb is the pain of the whole body. Sharing grief doesn’t double it, it halves it. Staying alone to look strong is carrying the load on one shoulder.

A table carried by two people is far lighter than one dragged by a single person.

You’re not alone. You just haven’t opened the door yet.
grief.body: Reach out to someone living through the same loss: a short message, a phone call. Saying “I was thinking of you” is enough.
grief.ask: Did you reach out to someone today? What did it leave in you?

grief.title: Leaves
grief.read:
The trees are shedding their leaves. They rustle under your feet as you walk, and you think about how temporary everything is.

Marcus Aurelius quotes an old poem: the wind scatters the leaves on the ground, and in spring the forest puts out new ones. So it is with the generations of men, he says; one goes, another comes.

This isn’t making death unimportant. Seeing loss not as an injustice but as part of nature’s order lifts some of the weight. Grief turns from the question “why” to the question “how.”

While the last leaf trembles on the branch, the roots under the soil are getting ready for a new spring.

Nothing disappears; it only changes form.
grief.body: Go outside and look at the season changing: the falling leaves, the shortening day, the sky. Without thinking about anything, just look.
grief.ask: As you watched the change in nature, what did you notice about your own loss?

grief.title: Carrying them
grief.read:
For a week you’ve been walking with your grief. The pain may not have lessened, but its shape has changed: it no longer only crushes; sometimes it turns into a warm memory.

Seneca writes that, in time, the memory of friends we have lost stops being bitter and grows sweet, just as a sour fruit ripens.

Finishing grief doesn’t mean forgetting. You don’t leave the one you love behind; you take them with you. As long as you carry their smile, their patience, one of their habits into your own life, they go on living too.

Someone who cooks their mother’s recipe on the same day every year fills the kitchen with her every time.

You haven’t lost them. They live in you now.
grief.body: Do one thing in their spirit: cook the food they loved, go to a place they loved, or do a kindness they would have done.
grief.ask: How did you carry them today? How has your grief changed over these seven days?

enough.title: What do you own?
enough.read:
You open your wardrobe and can’t find anything to wear. Yet the wardrobe is full. In the drawers: chargers you’ve never used, a gift still in its box, things you kept because “they’ll come in handy one day.”

Some things you own, and some things own you. You have to protect them, clean them, carry them, envy the new model when it comes out. Seneca says the poor man isn’t the one who has little, but the one who wants more.

Having enough doesn’t mean leaving everything behind to live in a cave. The Stoics didn’t forbid wealth; they only taught how not to be its slave. The problem isn’t owning things, it’s being owned.

Every item you put in a box when you move has a weight; some weigh more on your mind than on your arms.

Today, just look: what are you carrying, and what is carrying you?
enough.body: Write down ten things you own. Next to each one, ask: Does this serve me, or do I serve it? Mark the ones that wear you out.
enough.ask: Which thing on your list felt heavier than you expected?

enough.title: Rehearse poverty
enough.read:
Bills, rent, the chance of losing your job one day. Money worry usually comes not from going without, but from imagining going without.

Seneca gave a wealthy friend a strange piece of advice: for a few days each month, eat the plainest food, wear the roughest clothes, then ask yourself: is this what I was afraid of?

This isn’t self-punishment. The point isn’t to make yourself suffer, but to see the real size of the fear. Most people don’t know how good a simple meal can feel, because they’ve never tried it.

A slice of bread, a little cheese and a glass of water: to a hungry person, there’s no finer table.

Once you’ve met what you fear face to face, you stop fearing it quite so much.
enough.body: Eat one meal as simply as you can, or go a whole day without spending anything. At the end of the day, ask: what was missing?
enough.ask: What did the simple meal or the no-spend day leave in you? Was it as hard as you feared?

enough.title: The trick of comparison
enough.read:
A friend’s new car, someone else’s holiday on your screen, the neighbor’s remodeled kitchen. In the morning you needed nothing; by evening you fall asleep feeling something is missing.

We want most of the things we want because we’ve seen them in someone else. Things we might never want if we asked ourselves suddenly become necessities once they shine in someone else’s shop window.

People take this for envy, but often it isn’t; it’s a slip of attention. You stop looking at your own life and take someone else’s as the measure. And that measure changes every day; you can never catch up.

The runner who looks at the next lane misses their own stride.

When you come back to your own lane, you see how far you’ve come.
enough.body: When you notice you want something, stop and ask: Do I want this, or do I want it because I saw it on someone?
enough.ask: Which of your wants did you notice today was really born of a comparison?

enough.title: Nature’s measure
enough.read:
You add something to your cart. Do you really need it? Maybe. Or maybe just because it’s on sale, or to feel good for a moment.

Epictetus offers a simple measure: the foot is the measure of the shoe. You buy the shoe that fits your foot. Once you go past the measure, first you want a gilded one, then a purple one, then an embroidered one; there’s no end to it.

This measure isn’t poverty. What nature asks for is little and easy to find: food, shelter, warmth, a few friends. What’s endless is what appearances ask for. Whoever lives by nature will never be poor; whoever lives by other people’s opinions will never be rich.

A child can play happily all afternoon with the box the most expensive toy came in.

When you set the measure, what’s enough is enough for you.
enough.body: Before you buy something, ask yourself: Is this what I need asking, or what my image wants?
enough.ask: Where did you see the difference between need and image today?

enough.title: In your house, not your heart
enough.read:
A watch you love, maybe a book collection, maybe a beautiful home. Then one day it gets scratched, lost, broken, and your day goes dark.

Seneca was a very rich man, and he was criticized for it. His answer was this: the wise man keeps wealth in his house, not in his heart. Things serve him; he doesn’t serve them.

Having enough doesn’t mean turning your back on beautiful things. There’s a fine line between enjoying something and clinging to it. The one who enjoys looks at the present; the one who clings looks at the fear of losing it.

Someone who drinks coffee from a beautiful cup loves it every morning; when the cup breaks they’re sad, but their morning doesn’t break with it.

When you’re not afraid of losing, you truly enjoy what you have.
enough.body: Truly enjoy something you own, without wanting more of it or something better.
enough.ask: As you looked at what you were enjoying, was the fear of losing it there with you too?

enough.title: Giving
enough.read:
A coat in your wardrobe you never wear, a book on the shelf you’ve already read, an hour in your calendar you could give to someone. Somewhere, someone needs exactly those.

Seneca wrote a whole book on kindness. What he dwelt on most wasn’t what is given, but how: without expecting anything back, quietly, and without shaming the one who receives.

Giving looks like the opposite of having enough, but it’s two movements of the same muscle. You can give what you don’t hold too tightly; and the more you give, the more you see what you don’t need.

When you light one candle from another, your own flame loses nothing.

What you give doesn’t shrink; it leaves you and lives on in someone else.
enough.body: Quietly give something of your time or your things. Without telling anyone.
enough.ask: How did it feel to give quietly? Did anything feel missing?

enough.title: Enough
enough.read:
For a week you’ve been looking at what you own with different eyes. Maybe you gave a few things away, maybe you skipped a purchase, maybe you enjoyed a simple meal.

Wealth has no end; every step points to the next one. Enough, though, has a limit, but no one draws that limit for you. You’re the one who sets it.

Having enough isn’t not wanting; it’s choosing what you want. Whoever knows what is enough can want the rest or let it go; but they’re never dependent on it.

When you come back from a long walk and sit down on the doorstep, your tired legs and a glass of water feel worth more than anything in the world.

There’s already enough. Seeing that is the greatest wealth.
enough.body: Write an “enough for me” list: What do you already have? Which of these could be gone and still leave your peace in place?
enough.ask: Over these seven days, how has the word “enough” changed for you?
